title: Essay Writing
tagline: Composition · reading the topic, planning, structure and polish

sourceNote.boardprep: All notes, model openings and endings, vocabulary, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice and are not taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: An essay is a short, organised piece of writing that develops one central idea from a beginning to an end. Good marks come less from long sentences and rare words than from choosing the right approach to the topic, planning before you write, keeping paragraphs focused and finishing with a proper ending. This chapter shows you how to do each of these in the time you have.

learn.title: Reading the topic and choosing a type

blocks.text: Before you write a single line, read the topic twice and underline the key words. The wording of a topic usually tells you which kind of essay is wanted. If you choose the wrong kind, even fluent writing can drift away from what was asked.

items.meaning: Tells a story or an experience in time order. Typical topics: 'The Day the Lights Went Out', 'A Journey I Shall Never Forget'. Needs a clear beginning, a turning point and an ending that closes the story.

Paints a picture of a person, place, scene or event using the senses. Typical topics: 'A Crowded Railway Platform', 'The Old Banyan Tree'. Needs order (near to far, morning to night) and precise details.
Thinks about an idea, looking at several sides and often drawing on personal experience. Typical topics: 'Friendship', 'The Value of Silence'. Needs balanced points and a thoughtful conclusion.

Takes a position and defends it with reasons and examples. Typical topics: 'Homework should be abolished', 'Should schools ban sweets?'. Needs a clear stand, evidence and a fair look at the opposite view.

items: Look for verbs of instruction such as describe, argue, narrate, discuss or reflect.
A topic that starts with 'Should' or contains a claim almost always wants an argument.
A topic that names a single place, person or object usually wants a description.
If two types could fit, choose the one you can support with the best material, and stay with it.

blocks.text: A short plan protects you from the two commonest essay faults: running out of ideas halfway and wandering away from the topic. Three minutes spent on planning almost always saves more than three minutes of rewriting.

items: Minute one: underline the key words in the topic and decide the type of essay.
Minute one: write your central idea in a single sentence. Everything you write must serve it.
Minute two: jot down four or five points, examples or images in the margin. Do not write sentences yet.
Minute three: number the points in the order you will use them, and cross out anything weak or repeated.
Decide your first line and your last line now, so you never get stuck at either end.

items.meaning: Catches the reader and shows the direction of the essay. You can start with a striking scene, a question, a short statement of your view or a moment in the middle of the action. Avoid announcing 'In this essay I will write about'.
Two to four paragraphs, each built on one main idea. Begin with a clear topic sentence, add explanation, an example or a detail, and end by tying the point back to the topic.
Closes the essay with a feeling of completion. It may return to the opening image, state a lesson learnt or look ahead. Do not introduce a brand new point, and do not apologise for the essay.

items: One paragraph, one idea. When the idea changes, start a new paragraph.
Balance the parts: a huge middle with a two-line ending looks unfinished.
Do not leave a single sentence standing alone as a paragraph, unless it is a deliberate dramatic line in a narrative.
Leave a line or indent clearly so the paragraphs are easy to see.

learn.title: Linking words, vocabulary and sentence variety

blocks.text: Linking words make your ideas flow from sentence to sentence and from paragraph to paragraph. Use them to show a relationship, not simply to decorate the writing.

items.meaning: however, on the other hand, yet, nevertheless, whereas
because, since, therefore, as a result, consequently
at first, soon afterwards, meanwhile, eventually, at last
in short, on the whole, all things considered, finally

items: Vary the length of sentences. A short sentence after two long ones can land with real force.
Begin sentences in different ways: with a verb form, a time phrase, a subject or a linking word.
Choose the exact word, not the grandest one. 'Trudged' is better than 'walked slowly and tiredly'.
Use a word only if you are sure of its meaning and spelling.
Keep to one tense in a narrative unless the time really changes.

blocks.text: A cliche is a phrase used so often that it has lost its force. Examiners read many essays that begin 'Since time immemorial' or end 'Honesty is the best policy'. Replace such phrases with something specific from your own picture of the topic.

items.text: Weak: 'The sun was shining brightly and the birds were chirping.' Better: 'By seven, the tin roofs were already too hot to touch.'
items.note: A single exact detail is stronger than a stock picture.

items.text: Weak: 'We had a wonderful time and enjoyed a lot.' Better: 'By evening my cheeks ached from laughing.'
items.note: Show the result of the feeling instead of naming it.

items.text: Weak: 'In conclusion, we should all work hard.' Better: 'The next time a task looks too big, I shall remember the steep path and take it one bend at a time.'
items.note: Tie the ending to something you have actually written.

blocks.text: These are BoardPrep models, written to show technique. They are not full essays and should not be memorised. Notice how each opening begins inside the topic and how each ending returns to it.

MODEL 1 (narrative). Topic: An Evening Without Electricity. Opening: The lights went out just as I opened my geometry book. For a moment the whole house seemed to hold its breath; then the fans slowed, the fridge fell silent, and a dog began barking somewhere down the lane. Mother lit a candle and placed it in the middle of the table. I did not know it yet, but the next two hours would become the most memorable of that month.

MODEL 1 ending: When the lights returned, we blinked at them like strangers. Nobody rushed to switch on the television. I folded my geometry book, blew out the candle and realised that the darkness had shown me something the brightness never had: my family was worth listening to.

MODEL 2 (argumentative). Topic: Mobile phones should not be allowed in classrooms. Opening: Every school bag today carries a small glowing rectangle, and every teacher has a different opinion about it. Some call it a distraction; others call it a library in a pocket. I believe that phones should not be allowed in classrooms, though they need not be banned from school altogether. The reason is simple: learning needs attention, and attention is exactly what a phone divides.

MODEL 2 ending: To conclude, phones are useful tools but poor classmates. If schools keep them in bags during lessons and allow them at break for emergencies, students will lose little and gain a great deal of focus. A rule that protects attention is not an attack on technology; it is a defence of learning.
Keep the last two minutes for a calm read-through. Read slowly, and read what is written, not what you meant to write.

items: Does every sentence begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark?
Do subjects and verbs agree, and is the tense consistent?
Have you checked commonly confused words such as their and there, its and it's, affect and effect?
Is every paragraph about one idea, and does the essay stay on the topic?
Are there any run-on sentences that need to be split, or fragments that need to be completed?
Have you counted roughly against the word limit given in the question?
Is the handwriting clear? Correct mistakes neatly with a single line through the word.

keyPoints: Read the topic twice, underline the key words and decide the type of essay before writing.
A three-minute plan with one central sentence and four or five ordered points prevents wandering.
Use an opening that catches interest and an ending that closes the essay without new points.
One paragraph should carry one main idea, introduced by a clear topic sentence.
Linking words show relationships between ideas; use them with purpose.
Specific details are stronger than cliches and stock phrases.
Always leave time to proofread for spelling, punctuation, tense and agreement.
examFocus: Matching your approach to the topic: narrative, descriptive, reflective or argumentative.
Following the word limit given in the question.
Paragraph organisation and a logical order of ideas.
Accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation over the whole essay.
Range of vocabulary and variety of sentence structure.
A complete piece: it should have a proper opening and a proper ending.

vocabulary.meaning: in addition; also (used to add a stronger point)
vocabulary.context: The park is clean; moreover, it is the only green space within two kilometres of the school.
The climb was steep; nevertheless, we reached the top before noon.
The bridge was closed for repairs; consequently, buses were sent by the longer road.

vocabulary.meaning: producing strong, clear pictures in the mind
vocabulary.context: Her vivid description of the market made me smell the fresh coriander.

vocabulary.meaning: to walk slowly and heavily, as if tired
vocabulary.context: We trudged home through the mud after the match.

vocabulary.meaning: used to introduce a contrasting point of view
vocabulary.context: Homework builds discipline; on the other hand, too much of it leaves no time to play.

vocabulary.meaning: when looking back at a past event
vocabulary.context: In retrospect, missing the early bus was the best thing that happened that week.
A prompt reply from the principal settled the matter the same afternoon.
The lake was tranquil until the ducks arrived.

vocabulary.meaning: settling a question so that no doubt remains
vocabulary.context: The final example was conclusive proof that recycling saves money.

questions.prompt: Name the four common types of essay and state in one line what each type does.
questions.answer: Narrative essays tell a story or an experience in time order. Descriptive essays paint a picture of a person, place or scene using details of the senses. Reflective or discursive essays think about an idea from more than one side. Argumentative essays take a position and support it with reasons and examples.
questions.explanation: One mark for each type named with a correct function.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up reflective and argumentative essays. A reflective essay explores an idea; an argumentative essay defends a stand.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best opening sentence for a narrative essay called 'A Rainy Morning'?
options: In this essay I am going to write about a rainy morning.
Rain is a natural phenomenon that occurs all over the world.
The first drops hit the tin roof like a handful of coins, and I knew the bus would be late.
Everyone likes rain, and so do I.
questions.answer: The first drops hit the tin roof like a handful of coins, and I knew the bus would be late.
questions.explanation: It starts inside the scene, uses a fresh comparison and sets up the events to follow. The first option only announces the topic, the second is a textbook statement and the fourth is vague.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option that names the topic directly. Announcing the topic is not an opening.

questions.prompt: Improve this weak opening for an essay titled 'My Last School Picnic': 'In this essay I am going to write about my last school picnic. It was very nice and we enjoyed a lot.'
questions.answer: Model rewrite: The bus had barely left the gate when Mr. Kulkarni's tuneless singing began, and by the first bend the whole of Class IX had joined in. None of us guessed that the day at Silver Lake would end with all of us soaked, muddy and laughing.
questions.explanation: The original announces the topic, uses a vague word (nice) and a wrong idiom (enjoyed a lot). A better opening starts in the middle of the action, gives concrete detail and hints at what follows. Any rewrite that does these things earns credit. The names here are invented for the model.
questions.commonMistake: Only changing 'very nice' to 'very good'. The problem is the whole approach, not one word.

questions.prompt: Plan an essay on 'A Day at a Busy Railway Station' in five bullet points. State the type of essay first.
questions.answer:
Type: descriptive.
- Opening: the station at dawn, half asleep, the first tea stall lighting its stove.
- Sights and sounds: porters, announcements, whistles, the scramble as a train arrives.
- People: a family with too many bags, a student revising on a bench, a vendor calling out his goods.
- Contrast: the same platform at noon, hot and crowded, and late at night, almost empty.
- Ending: what the station taught me about how many separate lives cross for a few minutes.
questions.explanation: A good plan names the type, moves in a clear order (time is a natural order for a place) and includes concrete material as well as an ending. Five distinct, ordered points are needed.
questions.commonMistake: Writing five points that all say the same thing, such as 'the station is crowded'.

questions.prompt: Identify what is wrong with this paragraph from an essay on 'Healthy Habits': 'Exercise is good. Exercise is good for the heart. Sleep is also good and I sleep early. Food is important, eating fruit is important and I also like sweets, we should drink water because water is good.'
questions.answer: The paragraph has no single main idea and no topic sentence; it jumps from exercise to sleep to food to water. The word 'good' is repeated without any explanation. Sentences are very short and similar at the start, then a run-on sentence joins several ideas with commas. There are no linking words, no examples, and the remark about liking sweets does not fit the point. A better paragraph would focus on one habit, such as exercise, explain how it helps, and give an example.
questions.explanation: Mention lack of focus, repetition and vague vocabulary, poor sentence variety or run-on, missing linkers and lack of examples.
questions.commonMistake: Only correcting the punctuation. The deeper problems are organisation and development.

questions.prompt: Rewrite each of these cliches in a fresher way: (a) 'as busy as a bee'; (b) 'time flies'; (c) 'at the crack of dawn'.
questions.answer: (a) She hurried between the counter and the kitchen, never finishing one task before starting the next. (b) It felt as if I had only just sat down when the bell rang for the end of the day. (c) We left while the streetlamps were still on and the milkman was only beginning his round.
questions.explanation: Any specific rewrite that shows the idea through a detail, without repeating the stock phrase, earns credit.
questions.commonMistake: Replacing one cliche with another, such as 'as busy as an ant'.

questions.prompt: Write one sentence each using a linking word of (a) contrast, (b) result, (c) addition and (d) time sequence.
questions.answer: (a) The trek was tiring; however, the view made it worthwhile. (b) The stream had flooded; therefore, we returned by the main road. (c) The library is quiet; moreover, it has a fine collection of atlases. (d) At first the crowd was silent; soon afterwards, it broke into applause.
questions.explanation: One mark each for a sentence in which the linking word matches the relationship named and the sentence is punctuated correctly.
questions.commonMistake: Using 'but' and 'and' every time. Also joining two sentences with only a comma before 'however'.

questions.prompt: Write the concluding paragraph, in about 60 words, for an argumentative essay titled 'Every Student Should Learn a Musical Instrument'.
questions.answer: Music is not a luxury to be squeezed in after the serious subjects; it trains patience, memory and teamwork in a way few other activities can. A student who has practised a difficult passage a hundred times will not fear a difficult chapter. For these reasons, every school should give every student the chance to pick up an instrument and play.
questions.explanation: Marking guide: restates the stand without copying earlier sentences (1); gives a final reason or image (1); links to the topic (1); no new unsupported point (1); accurate language and roughly the given length (1).
questions.commonMistake: Beginning 'In conclusion, I would like to say that' and then repeating the introduction word for word.

questions.prompt: Decide the most suitable type of essay (narrative, descriptive, reflective or argumentative) for each topic and give a reason: (a) 'The Old Banyan Tree'; (b) 'Homework Should Be Abolished'; (c) 'A Journey I Shall Never Forget'; (d) 'The Value of Silence'.
questions.answer: (a) Descriptive, because it names one object and asks for a picture of it. (b) Argumentative, because it makes a claim that can be supported or opposed. (c) Narrative, because a journey is an experience told in time order. (d) Reflective, because it invites thought about an abstract idea rather than a story or a stand.
questions.explanation: One mark for each correct type with a reason drawn from the wording of the topic.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the type without any reason.

questions.prompt: Explain what a topic sentence is and why each development paragraph needs one. Give an example for an essay on 'The Importance of Reading'.
questions.answer: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph, usually in the first sentence, and tells the reader what the paragraph will prove or describe. Without it a paragraph may wander. Example: 'Reading widens our vocabulary long before we notice that it has done so.' The rest of the paragraph would then explain and illustrate this claim.
questions.explanation: One mark for the definition, one for its purpose and one for a suitable example that makes a single, clear point.
questions.commonMistake: Writing a topic sentence that is too broad or that contains two different ideas.

questions.prompt: A student's essay ends: 'And that is all I have to say. I hope you liked my essay. I also forgot to mention that plastic is bad for the sea.' Explain three faults in this ending and rewrite it for an essay on 'Plastic Pollution'.
questions.answer: Faults: it apologises and asks for approval instead of closing with confidence; it treats the essay as unfinished; and it introduces a new point at the last moment. Rewrite: We cannot clean the sea with regret, but we can stop feeding it. Each bag refused, each bottle refilled and each careless habit corrected keeps one more piece of plastic out of the waves. The change begins at home, at the next shopping trip.
questions.explanation: Marks for three faults named (3) and an ending that is confident, tied to the topic and free of new points (2).
questions.commonMistake: Rewriting the ending but leaving a new point or a request for approval in it.
